title: EVIDENCE-BASED HUMAN-CENTRIC LIGHTING ASSIST TOOL TOWARDS A HEALTHIER LIT ENVIRONMENT
research_question: How to equip lighting designers and architects with accessible and affordable tools to evaluate critical parameters related to non-visual aspects of light exposures at the individual level in the building?

participants.description: Overall: 51 participants aged 31-60 years (23 female, 28 male). Spectrometer field study: 2 office workers (male: 36 years, female: 36 years) in Seattle, WA. Dashboard development: Phase 1 (Relevance Cycle) 34 participants (19 lighting designers, 15 office workers). Phase 3 (Design Cycle) 15 participants (5 for low-fidelity, 5 for medium-fidelity, 5 for high-fidelity prototypes) plus 2 expert reviewers for medium-fidelity.
participants.recruitment: Participants for the field study volunteered. Participants for the dashboard usability testing were recruited from previous participants in the relevance cycle.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Experiment 1: 30 LEDs (various colors) in a controlled dark laboratory environment, measured in an integrated sphere. Experiment 2: 106 different light sources (54 LEDs, 5 Fluorescent, 11 Incandescent, 3 Halogen, 33 daylight samples) in a semi-real-world environment, measured in an integrated sphere. Experiment 3: 40 real-world lighting conditions (30 indoors, 10 outdoors) including warm/cool LEDs, daylight, and mixed light, with various colored background surfaces (red, blue, green, yellow). Field Study: Home-office environment with a West-facing window, warm LED (2700K) for Day 1-6, and an ilumi BR30 Bluetooth LED Smart bulb (2700K-6500K) for Day 7-8. Blind conditions varied (fully retracted, fully closed, adaptable).
Low-fidelity, medium-fidelity, and high-fidelity prototypes of an interactive dashboard for visualizing lighting data.

measures.instrument: Developed low-cost wearable spectrometer (AS7265X spectral sensor), Ocean Insight WaveGo light spectrum meter (reference), AvaSpec-Mini2048CL spectrometer (reference)
Normalized Root-Mean-Square Error (NRMSE), Root-Mean-Square Error (RMSE), Sum of Squared Errors (SSE), Correlation Coefficient (R-value), Maximum Error
Calculated from SPD using Rea et al. mathematical model
High Dynamic Range Image (HDRI) sensors with fisheye cameras, false-color luminance mapping
Semi-structured interviews, observations, content analysis, rainbow spreadsheet

mechanisms: Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) improve the accuracy of low-cost spectral sensors by learning patterns in Spectral Power Distribution (SPD) data.
Downsampling and normalizing SPD data reduces the output size of the ANN model and decreases the effect of noises, thereby increasing speed and accuracy.
Non-linear activation functions (Tansig, Logsig) are more effective than linear functions for learning complex features in SPD data.
The Trainlm Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm is an efficient method for training ANNs with non-linear characteristics.
MLP models can be under-fitted (too few neurons) or over-fitted (too many neurons), affecting their accuracy.
Dynamic electric lighting and daylight significantly impact the circadian stimulus potential of indoor lighting.
Increased distance from a window reduces Circadian Stimulus (CS) due to limited penetration depths of daylight.
Individual differences in sleep-wake patterns and work schedules contribute to variations in personal lighting conditions and their circadian effectiveness.
A user-centered design approach, involving end-users throughout the development process, leads to a more usable, useful, and acceptable interactive dashboard.
moderators: Type of light source (electric light vs. daylight) on ANN accuracy.
Participant's daily schedule (sleep, waking, working hours) on mean CS levels.
Time of day (morning, afternoon, evening, night) on mean CS levels.
Individual participant identity (e.g., Participant 1 vs. Participant 2) on mean CS levels.
Distance to window on mean CS levels from daylight.
implementation_implications: The developed low-cost, wearable spectrometer can be integrated into IoT-based intelligent lighting systems to tailor indoor lighting conditions according to individual circadian needs in real-time.
The spectrometer can serve as a 'dosimeter' for continuous monitoring of spectral irradiance in various settings, including long-term care facilities for light therapy.

The interactive dashboard provides non-expert users with meaningful and easy-to-understand information about circadian-effective lighting, enabling them to manage their health and promote healthy behavior change.
The tool can be a valuable resource for lighting designers and architects for post-design evaluation of buildings, promoting healthier lit environments.
The system can be used as a connected technology with an app to monitor how light affects individuals' health and provide tips for controlling living conditions.

limitations: Limited number of light sources (30 in Experiment 1, 106 in Experiment 2) used for ANN training, potentially limiting generalization to all types of light sources.
Limited ANNs architectures, activation functions, and learning algorithms were explored for MLP training.
The accuracy of the MLP model decreases when exposed to unique and complex SPDs, particularly daylight, compared to known patterns.
The field study had a limited number of participants (N=2) due to the COVID-19 pandemic, restricting the investigation of inter-individual differences.
The field study was conducted in summer, and results regarding circadian-effective light levels may vary in other seasons or geographical locations.

Usability testing of the interactive dashboard was conducted with a small sample size (5 participants per prototype iteration), which might not identify all usability issues or significant differences in SUS scores.
The usability testing was limited to medium- and high-fidelity prototypes, not a fully functional application, due to funding constraints.
